name: Richter Energy Release
description: Estimates the seismic energy radiated by an earthquake from its magnitude using the Gutenberg-Richter energy relation. Because it is exponential, each unit of magnitude corresponds to about 31.6 times more energy.
notes: Result is in joules and grows very rapidly, so small magnitude errors change energy greatly. The constants apply to the classic energy-magnitude relation, not moment magnitude directly.

name: Moment Magnitude
description: Converts the seismic moment of an earthquake into the moment magnitude scale using the standard logarithmic relation. Seismic moment measures the size of an earthquake as the product of fault area, average slip, and rock rigidity.
notes: Seismic moment must be in newton-meters and uses base-10 logarithm. Moment magnitude is preferred over the Richter scale for large earthquakes because it does not saturate.

name: Earthquake Energy Ratio
description: Computes how many times more energy one earthquake releases than another from the difference in their magnitudes. It applies the rule that each magnitude unit corresponds to about 31.6 times more radiated energy.
notes: The result is a dimensionless multiple; a difference of 2 magnitudes gives roughly 1000 times the energy. Sign matters, since m1 minus m2 sets the direction of comparison.

name: Slope Grade (Percent)
description: Expresses the steepness of a slope as a percent grade by dividing vertical rise by horizontal run and multiplying by 100. A 100 percent grade corresponds to a 45-degree slope where rise equals run.
notes: Rise and run must share the same length unit. Percent grade is not the same as the slope angle in degrees; the two coincide only near zero.

name: Slope Angle
description: Converts a slope's vertical rise and horizontal run into an inclination angle in degrees using the arctangent of their ratio. It gives the true angle the slope makes with the horizontal.
notes: Rise and run in the same length unit; the arctangent returns radians, which the factor 180 over pi converts to degrees. Angle stays below 90 degrees for any finite run.

name: Grade to Angle
description: Converts a percent grade into a slope angle in degrees by taking the arctangent of the grade divided by 100. It translates the road-sign style steepness figure into a geometric angle.
notes: Grade is entered as a percent, so 100 percent maps to 45 degrees. Output is in degrees; the relationship is nonlinear, so doubling the grade does not double the angle.

name: Hypocentral Distance from S-P Interval (Omori's Formula)
description: Estimates the distance from a seismograph station to an earthquake's hypocenter (focus) using Omori's formula, k*(ts-tp), from the S-P arrival time interval. The larger the delay between P- and S-wave arrivals, the farther the hypocenter.
notes: The constant k depends on local crustal velocity structure and is commonly taken near 8 km/s, though regional values vary from about 7 to 9. ts and tp must be in seconds.

name: Airy Isostasy Root
description: Computes the depth of the crustal root beneath topography under Airy isostasy, where mountains are supported by buoyant crustal material extending into the denser mantle. The root depth equals the crustal density times height, divided by the density contrast between mantle and crust.
notes: Densities must share the same unit and rhom must exceed rhoc for a positive root. This assumes local (Airy) compensation with a constant-density crust of uniform composition.

name: Pratt Isostasy Density
description: Computes the column density under Pratt isostasy, where topography is compensated by lateral density variations above a common depth of compensation. Higher topography h corresponds to a lower density rho0·D/(D+h) so that all columns exert equal pressure at depth D.
notes: D and h use the same length unit; taller columns must be less dense. Contrasts with Airy isostasy, which instead varies crustal thickness at constant density.

name: Geothermal Gradient Temperature
description: Computes the temperature at depth z by adding the geothermal gradient G times depth to the surface temperature T0. It assumes temperature rises linearly with depth.
notes: G is in °C per metre, so with a typical 25 °C/km use 0.025; z is in metres. The linear model ignores variations in thermal conductivity and heat sources.

name: International Gravity Formula (1980)
description: Computes normal (theoretical) gravity at sea level as a function of latitude using the 1980 International Gravity Formula. It captures how gravity increases from about 9.780 m/s² at the equator to roughly 9.832 m/s² at the poles due to Earth's rotation and flattening.
notes: Latitude phi must be in radians. This gives the reference ellipsoid gravity at sea level, excluding elevation and terrain (free-air and Bouguer) corrections.

name: Free-Air Gravity Correction
description: Computes the free-air correction applied to gravity measurements to account for the decrease of gravity with elevation above the reference ellipsoid. It adds 0.3086 mGal for each metre of elevation h.
notes: h is in metres and the result is in milligals (mGal). This corrects only for height in free air; it does not account for the mass of rock below the station (Bouguer correction).

name: Bouguer Slab Correction
description: Computes the Bouguer slab correction, which accounts for the gravitational attraction of the rock mass between the measurement station and the reference level, modeled as an infinite horizontal slab. It equals 0.04193 mGal per unit density and metre of thickness.
notes: Density rho must be in g/cm³ and thickness h in metres to yield milligals with this coefficient. It is subtracted from the free-air anomaly; terrain corrections are separate.

name: P-Wave Velocity
description: Computes the velocity of compressional (P) seismic waves in an elastic medium from its bulk modulus K, shear modulus mu, and density rho. It equals the square root of (K + 4/3·mu) divided by density.
notes: All inputs in SI units (Pa and kg/m³) give velocity in m/s. P-waves are always faster than S-waves in the same medium because of the added bulk-modulus term.

name: S-Wave Velocity
description: Computes the velocity of shear (S) seismic waves in an elastic medium as the square root of the shear modulus mu divided by density rho. Because fluids have zero shear modulus, S-waves cannot travel through them.
notes: Inputs in SI units (Pa and kg/m³) give velocity in m/s. S-waves are always slower than P-waves in the same solid material.

name: Poisson's Ratio (from Vp/Vs)
description: Computes Poisson's ratio of an elastic medium from its P-wave and S-wave velocities. The dimensionless ratio characterizes how much the material contracts laterally when stretched and depends only on the Vp/Vs ratio.
notes: Vp and Vs must share the same unit; the result is dimensionless. Poisson's ratio typically lies between 0 and 0.5 for common rocks, with 0.5 indicating a fluid-like medium.

name: Radiometric Age (Isochron)
description: Computes the radiometric age of a sample from the ratio of accumulated daughter isotope D to remaining parent isotope P, using the radioactive decay law. The age equals ln(1 + D/P) divided by the decay constant lambda.
notes: D and P share the same unit so their ratio is dimensionless; lambda is in 1/yr, giving age in years. Assumes a closed system with no initial daughter isotope.

name: Geomagnetic Dipole Field
description: Computes the total magnetic field strength of a geocentric dipole at radius r and magnetic latitude lat. The field falls off as 1/r³ and varies with latitude through the factor sqrt(1 + 3·sin²(lat)), being twice as strong at the poles as at the equator.
notes: Use SI units with r in metres and lat in radians; result is in tesla. This idealizes Earth's field as a pure centered dipole, ignoring higher-order and crustal components.

name: Curie Depth
description: Computes the Curie depth, the depth at which rock reaches the Curie temperature and loses its ferromagnetism, using a linear geothermal gradient. It divides the temperature rise from surface T0 to Curie point Tc by the gradient G.
notes: Tc and T0 are in °C and G in °C per metre, so use 0.025 for 25 °C/km; result is in metres. Assumes a constant gradient with no heat-production variation.

name: Gravity at Depth (uniform Earth)
description: Computes gravity at depth z inside an Earth of uniform density, where gravity decreases linearly from the surface value g0 to zero at the center. It multiplies g0 by (R − z)/R.
notes: R and z use the same length unit and z must not exceed R. The linear decrease holds only for a hypothetical uniform-density sphere; the real Earth's gravity actually rises slightly before falling.

name: Flexural Rigidity
description: Computes the flexural rigidity of an elastic plate, a measure of its resistance to bending, from Young's modulus Em, elastic thickness Te, and Poisson's ratio nu. Rigidity scales with the cube of thickness, so it is very sensitive to Te.
notes: Use SI units (Em in Pa, Te in m) to get rigidity in N·m; nu is dimensionless. The strong Te³ dependence means small thickness errors greatly affect the result.

name: Flexural Parameter
description: Computes the flexural parameter, the characteristic horizontal length scale over which an elastic lithospheric plate bends under a load. It is the fourth root of 4 times flexural rigidity Dr divided by the product of density contrast drho and gravity.
notes: Use SI units so the result is in metres; drho is the density difference between the material filling the flexure and that displaced beneath. Larger rigidity gives a broader, gentler deflection.

name: Postglacial Rebound Relaxation
description: Computes the remaining vertical displacement during postglacial rebound as the initial displacement u0 decays exponentially over time. After each relaxation time trel the displacement falls to about 37% (1/e) of its value.
notes: t and trel must use the same time unit; the result shares the length unit of u0. This single-exponential model idealizes the mantle as a single-viscosity Maxwell material.

name: Acoustic Impedance
description: Computes the acoustic (seismic) impedance of a material as the product of its density rho and wave velocity V. Impedance governs how much seismic energy is reflected at boundaries between layers.
notes: Use SI units (kg/m³ and m/s) to get impedance in kg/(m²·s). Contrasts in impedance between adjacent layers, not their absolute values, control seismic reflection strength.

name: Reflection Coefficient (normal incidence)
description: Computes the seismic reflection coefficient at normal incidence from the acoustic impedances of two layers as (Z2 − Z1)/(Z2 + Z1). It gives the fraction of wave amplitude reflected at the interface.
notes: Z1 and Z2 must share the same unit; the dimensionless result ranges from −1 to 1, where a negative value indicates a polarity reversal (reflection off a lower-impedance layer).

name: Critical Angle (Refraction)
description: Computes the critical angle of incidence at which a seismic wave passing from a slower layer (velocity V1) into a faster layer (V2) refracts along the interface. It equals the arcsine of V1/V2.
notes: Requires V2 greater than V1 so that V1/V2 is below 1; the result is in radians. Beyond this angle the wave is totally internally reflected and head waves form.

name: Earth Mass from Surface Gravity
description: Computes the mass of the Earth (or any planet) from its surface gravity g and radius R by inverting Newton's law of gravitation: mass equals g·R² divided by the gravitational constant G. It treats the body as a sphere.
notes: Use SI units (m/s², m) to get mass in kilograms. Assumes a spherically symmetric body; g here is the true gravitational acceleration, excluding rotation effects.

name: Adiabatic Temperature Gradient
description: Computes the adiabatic temperature gradient inside a convecting body, the rate at which temperature changes with depth when material moves without exchanging heat. It equals the thermal expansion coefficient alpha times gravity times temperature, divided by specific heat cp.
notes: Use SI units with T in kelvin; the result is in K/m and represents the background gradient in vigorously convecting regions such as the mantle or a stellar interior.

name: Thermal Diffusion Length
description: Computes the thermal diffusion length, the characteristic distance heat conducts in a given time t through a material of thermal diffusivity kappa. It equals the square root of kappa times t.
notes: Use SI units (m²/s and s) to get length in metres. It is an order-of-magnitude scale for how far a thermal signal penetrates, not a sharp boundary.

name: Geomagnetic Inclination
description: Computes the geomagnetic inclination, the angle at which the magnetic field dips below horizontal, from the geomagnetic latitude using the dipole relation tan(I) = 2·tan(latitude). The field is horizontal at the magnetic equator and vertical at the poles.
notes: Latitude is in radians and the result is inclination in radians. Valid for a geocentric axial dipole field, ignoring non-dipole and local anomalies.

name: Seismic Attenuation (Q)
description: Computes the amplitude of a seismic wave after traveling a distance x through a medium with quality factor Q, accounting for anelastic energy loss. The initial amplitude A0 decays exponentially, faster at higher frequency f and lower Q.
notes: Use SI units (x in m, V in m/s, f in Hz); Q and the amplitude ratio are dimensionless. Lower Q means stronger attenuation, so high frequencies are lost fastest with distance.

name: Gravitational Binding Energy (uniform sphere)
description: Computes the gravitational binding energy of a uniform-density sphere, the energy needed to disperse its mass to infinity against self-gravity. It equals 3·G·M² divided by 5·R.
notes: Use SI units (kg, m) to get energy in joules. Assumes constant density; a centrally condensed body like a real planet or star has larger binding energy for the same mass and radius.

name: Shear Modulus from S-wave Velocity
description: Computes the shear (rigidity) modulus of a rock or material from its bulk density and shear (S-wave) seismic velocity, mu = rho*Vs^2. It measures resistance to shape-distorting shear stress.
notes: Density and velocity must be in SI units (kg/m^3 and m/s) so the result comes out in pascals. Assumes an isotropic, elastic medium, as is standard in seismic velocity analysis.

name: Terrestrial Heat Flow (Fourier's Law)
description: Computes conductive terrestrial heat flow via Fourier's law, q = k·(dT/dz), combining rock thermal conductivity with the geothermal gradient (temperature rise per kilometre of depth).
notes: With conductivity in W/(m·K) and gradient in K/km, the product gives heat flow directly in mW/m^2, matching typical continental values of 40-90 mW/m^2. Assumes purely conductive, steady-state heat transport with no fluid advection.

name: Bulk Modulus from Vp, Vs, Density
description: Computes the bulk modulus of a material from density and its P-wave and S-wave seismic velocities, K = rho*(Vp^2 - (4/3)*Vs^2). It gives resistance to uniform (volumetric) compression.
notes: Density and both velocities must be in SI units for a result in pascals. Assumes an isotropic elastic medium; Vp must sufficiently exceed Vs for a physically meaningful positive bulk modulus.

name: Seismic Moment
description: Computes the seismic moment of an earthquake, a physical measure of its size, as the product of the crustal shear modulus mu, the rupture area A, and the average fault slip D. Larger rupture area or slip yields a proportionally larger moment.
notes: Use SI units (Pa, m², m) to get moment in newton-metres. Seismic moment scales linearly with area and slip, unlike magnitude which is logarithmic.

name: Seismic Energy (Gutenberg-Richter)
description: Estimates the radiated seismic energy of an earthquake from its magnitude M using the Gutenberg-Richter energy relation 10^(4.8 + 1.5·M). Energy rises by a factor of about 32 for each unit increase in magnitude.
notes: M is the dimensionless magnitude and the result is in joules. This is an empirical estimate of radiated energy and differs from the moment-based magnitude definition.

name: Stress Drop (circular fault)
description: Estimates the static stress drop of an earthquake on a circular fault from its seismic moment M0 and fault radius r, using the Eshelby relation (7/16)*M0/r^3. The result, in pascals, measures how much shear stress was released along the rupture.
notes: Assumes a circular crack in a uniform elastic medium. Because it scales as 1/r^3, small errors in the radius strongly affect the result; typical crustal earthquakes give a few MPa.

name: Brune Corner Frequency
description: Computes the corner frequency of an earthquake source spectrum from the S-wave velocity Vs and source radius r using Brune's model, fc = 0.37*Vs/r. The corner frequency marks where the displacement spectrum begins to fall off and reflects source size.
notes: Larger sources give lower corner frequencies. The 0.37 constant is specific to Brune's circular source model; other models use different coefficients, so values are model-dependent.

name: Source Radius (Brune)
description: Inverts Brune's model to estimate the earthquake source radius from the S-wave velocity Vs and the observed corner frequency fc, as r = 0.37*Vs/fc. Lower corner frequencies imply larger rupture areas.
notes: The inverse of the corner-frequency relation; uses the same 0.37 Brune constant. Corner frequency must come from the S-wave spectrum for consistency, and results are sensitive to how fc is picked.

name: Distance from S-P Time
description: Estimates the distance to an earthquake source from the S-minus-P arrival time difference dt and the P- and S-wave velocities, as dt*Vp*Vs/(Vp - Vs). The later-arriving S wave lags the P wave more with distance.
notes: Assumes a straight ray path through a uniform-velocity medium, so it is an approximation for shallow, nearby events. Requires Vp greater than Vs; result is a hypocentral distance.

name: Omori-Utsu Aftershock Rate
description: Gives the rate of aftershocks per day at time t after a mainshock using the modified Omori (Omori-Utsu) law, K/(c + t)^p. Aftershock frequency decays with time governed by the productivity K, time offset c, and exponent p.
notes: Time t and offset c are in days; the rate is per day. The exponent p is typically near 1, and c prevents the singularity at t = 0 shortly after the mainshock.

name: Gutenberg-Richter Frequency
description: Computes the number of earthquakes with magnitude at least M from the Gutenberg-Richter relation, 10^(a - b*M). The a-value sets overall seismicity and the b-value sets how quickly frequency drops with increasing magnitude.
notes: Gives cumulative frequency (events of magnitude M or greater), typically over a set time and region embedded in a. A b-value near 1 means each unit magnitude increase makes events about ten times rarer.

name: Local Magnitude (Southern California)
description: Calculates Richter local magnitude ML from a Wood-Anderson seismograph amplitude A (in mm) and epicentral distance D using the Southern California calibration of Hutton and Boore (1987), log(A) + 1.11*log(D) + 0.00189*D + 0.591. The distance terms correct for wave attenuation.
notes: Amplitude A is in mm on a Wood-Anderson instrument and distance D in km; log is base-10. The coefficients are calibrated for Southern California and are not universal.

name: Body-Wave Magnitude
description: Determines the body-wave magnitude mb from the ground-motion amplitude A, its period T, and a distance-depth calibration term Q, as log(A/T) + Q. It uses the amplitude-to-period ratio of teleseismic P waves.
notes: Amplitude A is in micrometres and period T in seconds; Q depends on distance and focal depth from standard tables. mb tends to saturate for very large earthquakes.

name: Surface-Wave Magnitude
description: Computes the surface-wave magnitude Ms from the ground amplitude A, period T, and epicentral distance D using log(A/T) + 1.66*log(D) + 3.3. It is based on long-period Rayleigh waves around 20 s period.
notes: Amplitude A is in micrometres, period T in seconds, and distance D in degrees. The formula is intended for shallow events with periods near 20 s; deep earthquakes are underestimated.

name: PGA Attenuation (simplified)
description: Estimates peak ground acceleration in g from a simplified attenuation (ground-motion) relation, a*exp(b*M)/R^c, where magnitude M raises PGA exponentially and distance R reduces it by geometric spreading with exponent c.
notes: The coefficients a, b, c are empirical and region-specific placeholders, not universal values. Real ground-motion models add saturation, site, and depth terms; this is a schematic form only.

name: Rupture Length (Wells-Coppersmith)
description: Estimates the surface rupture length of a fault in kilometres from earthquake magnitude M using the Wells and Coppersmith empirical regression, 10^(-3.22+0.69*M). Larger magnitudes correspond to longer ruptures.
notes: Empirical relation from a global dataset; coefficients here are for all fault types and give a mean estimate with real scatter. Result is surface rupture length in km, not subsurface rupture.

name: Rupture Area (Wells-Coppersmith)
description: Estimates the rupture area of a fault in square kilometres from earthquake magnitude M using the Wells and Coppersmith regression, 10^(-3.49+0.91*M). Rupture area grows rapidly with magnitude.
notes: Empirical mean relation with real scatter; coefficients are for all fault types combined. Output is subsurface rupture area in km^2, useful for fault source characterization.

name: Average Slip (Wells-Coppersmith)
description: Estimates the average coseismic slip on a fault in metres from earthquake magnitude M using the Wells and Coppersmith regression, 10^(-4.80+0.69*M). It gives the mean displacement across the rupture surface.
notes: Empirical mean with substantial scatter; represents average, not maximum, slip. Coefficients combine all fault types and should not be treated as exact for a single event.

name: Earthquake Recurrence Interval
description: Computes the average recurrence interval between large earthquakes on a fault as the coseismic slip D divided by the long-term slip rate s. It is the time needed to reaccumulate the slip released in one event.
notes: Slip D is in metres and slip rate s in metres per year, giving years. Assumes a characteristic-earthquake model where each event releases the same slip at a steady rate.

name: Seismic Moment Rate
description: Computes the rate at which seismic moment accumulates on a fault from the shear modulus mu, fault area A, and slip rate sr, as mu*A*sr. It quantifies how fast tectonic loading builds up moment available for future earthquakes.
notes: Uses SI units: mu in Pa, area in m^2, slip rate in m/yr, giving N·m per year. Represents the geodetic moment budget, which released seismicity should balance over time.

name: Energy Magnitude
description: Converts the radiated seismic energy En in joules into an energy magnitude Me using the Choy-Boatwright relation, (2/3)*(log(En) - 4.4). It expresses the earthquake's radiated energy on the magnitude scale.
notes: Energy En is in joules and log is base-10. Energy magnitude reflects radiated energy and can differ from moment magnitude, which reflects static fault displacement.

name: Rupture Duration
description: Estimates the time an earthquake rupture takes to propagate along a fault as the rupture length L divided by the rupture velocity Vr. It gives an order-of-magnitude duration of the faulting process.
notes: Length L is in metres and rupture velocity Vr in metres per second, giving seconds. Assumes unilateral rupture at constant speed; typical Vr is 70-90 percent of the shear-wave velocity.

name: Anelastic Attenuation (amplitude)
description: Gives the seismic wave amplitude after geometric spreading and anelastic attenuation, A0/R*exp(-pi*f*R/(Q*V)). The 1/R term is spreading and the exponential term is energy loss governed by the quality factor Q.
notes: Distance R and velocity V in SI, frequency f in Hz; the dimensionless Q measures how little energy is lost per cycle. Higher frequencies and lower Q attenuate faster.

name: Instrumental Intensity (Wald)
description: Estimates the instrumental Modified Mercalli Intensity from peak ground acceleration using Wald et al.'s regression, 3.66*log(PGA) - 1.66. It maps recorded shaking onto the felt-intensity scale.
notes: PGA is in cm/s^2 (gal) and log is base-10. Valid roughly for intensities V-VIII; at low and very high intensities velocity-based relations are used instead.

name: Fault Slip from Stress Drop
description: Estimates the average fault slip from the stress drop ds, a characteristic fault dimension L, and the shear modulus mu, as ds*L/mu. Slip scales with how much stress was released over the rupture size.
notes: All quantities in SI: stress drop and shear modulus in Pa, dimension in m, giving slip in metres. This is a scaling relation with an order-unity geometric factor omitted.

name: b-value (Aki-Utsu)
description: Estimates the Gutenberg-Richter b-value using the Aki-Utsu maximum-likelihood formula, log(e)/(Mmean - Mmin), from the mean magnitude and the minimum (completeness) magnitude of a catalog.
notes: log(e) is the base-10 log of Euler's number (about 0.4343); magnitudes are dimensionless. The minimum magnitude must be the catalog completeness threshold for the estimate to be unbiased.

name: Duration Magnitude
description: Computes a coda duration magnitude Md from the signal duration and epicentral distance using a + b*log(dur) + c*D. It uses how long the earthquake coda lasts instead of peak amplitude.
notes: Duration is in seconds, distance D in km, and log is base-10; coefficients a, b, c are network-specific calibrations. Useful for small local events where amplitude clips or saturates.

name: Stock-Tank Oil Initially in Place
description: Gives the volume of oil in a reservoir measured at surface conditions by the volumetric method (7758 barrels per acre-foot).
notes: Only a fraction (the recovery factor) can be produced.

name: Archie Water Saturation
description: Gives the share of pore space filled with water from resistivity logs (Archie 1942); the rest holds hydrocarbons.
notes: Valid for clean (shale-free) sandstones.

name: Hydrostatic Mud Pressure
description: Gives the bottom-hole pressure exerted by a column of drilling mud in oilfield units.
notes: Must exceed formation pressure to prevent a kick.

name: Arps Hyperbolic Production Decline
description: Gives a well's production rate over time with Arps' hyperbolic decline (1945); b = 0 is exponential decline.
notes: Shale wells often show b near or above 1 early on.

name: Blasting Powder Factor
description: Gives the explosive used per cubic metre of rock broken, a key blast-design figure.
notes: Typically 0.2–0.8 kg/m³ depending on rock hardness.

name: Open-Pit Stripping Ratio
description: Gives the tonnes of waste that must be moved per tonne of ore in an open-pit mine.
notes: The economic limit depends on ore value and mining cost.

name: Gravity at Altitude
description: Gives gravitational acceleration at height h above the surface from the inverse-square law.
notes: At the International Space Station (400 km) gravity is still about 89 % of its surface value.
